2: A magnet’s shape gives a clue to its use. A long bar is easy to hold and turn. A ring can slide over a rod. Shape alone, however, does not tell you how strong a magnet is. Compare what the magnets can actually do.
3: Test a part of the object whose material you know. A pencil may have a metal ferrule, and a sharpener may have a steel blade inside a plastic body. If only one part sticks, record that part rather than calling the whole object magnetic.

An object that does not stick may simply be too far from the magnet. Bring the magnet close without forcing the object against it. If a result surprises you, repeat the test and compare it with a known steel paper clip.
4: Coins and keys can give different results because they are made from different metals or mixtures. Test your own examples rather than guessing from their colour. A shiny surface does not tell you whether the material underneath is magnetic.
Compare two objects using the same magnet at the same distance. If you change both the object and the magnet, you cannot tell which change caused a different result.

A non-magnetic covering can hide a magnetic material. For example, a plastic-coated steel clip may still be attracted. This does not show that the plastic is magnetic; it shows that the magnet can act on the steel inside.
5: Compare the pattern before and after gently tapping the paper. Tapping helps grains move; it does not create poles. Keep the amount of filings and the paper position the same.
6: The letters N and S are a useful record of the poles. If the letters rub off, the poles remain. You can identify them again by comparing the magnet with a marked magnet or by letting it turn freely.
7: Let the magnet turn without touching the table, floor or stand. A twisted thread can pull it away from its resting direction. If the result changes between trials, check the suspension and remove nearby magnetic objects before deciding that the magnet behaves differently.
Repeated observations are useful because one trial can be disturbed. Draw the line after each trial in your notebook and compare your records.
8: A compass direction is a local observation. Nearby iron and other magnets can change it. That is why checking the surroundings is part of the experiment, just as important as waiting for the magnet to stop.
9: The compass needle turns; the letters printed on the dial do not. Turning the case brings those letters into line with the settled needle. If you carry the compass to another place or turn yourself around, let the needle settle and check the dial again.
A compass shows direction relative to the local magnetic field. Accurate map navigation also allows for the difference between magnetic north and geographic north.
Keep the compass level while reading it. A tilted needle may catch against its support or case. If it seems stuck, put the compass on a flat surface and wait before trusting the direction it shows.
11: Compare the two designs by asking the same questions: what is magnetised, what supports it, and what prevents it from turning freely? These questions explain why a floating needle fails if its cork touches the side of the bowl.
12: The round pencils reduce rubbing between magnet A and the table. Without them, the magnetic force might be present but too weak to overcome the friction. A magnet that does not move immediately has not necessarily stopped exerting a force.
13: Test both ends. If the first end attracts, turn the test bar around and try its other end against the same pole of your known magnet. Repulsion in either trial identifies a magnet. This is why a single observation of attraction is not enough.
16: In each game, name the object that feels the magnetic force. The card, water or glass can lie between the magnet and that object. Moving the magnet farther away may make the effect too weak to move the object, even when the material between them has not changed.

For the racing cars, identify the two ends that face each other before you let the cars move. Then turn just one magnet around. This changes the facing poles while keeping the cars and their wheels the same.
In a clip chain, the nearby magnet induces magnetisation in the clips. Remove it and compare the chain: some steel may retain magnetisation, so do not prescribe that every chain must fall apart.
17: The soft-iron pieces used for storage are called keepers. They join unlike poles across each end of the pair. This arrangement is useful for traditional school bar magnets; different modern magnets may come with their own storage instructions.
18: Explain these differences to a partner: a magnet and a magnetic material; attraction and repulsion; a prediction and an observation. Give one example from an activity for each pair.
